newsitem.title: UK: Labour's Blair to offer British voters a "contract".
newsitem.headline: Labour's Blair to offer British voters a "contract".

text.p: Labour Party leader Tony Blair will offer British voters a "contract", hoping to convince them he will keep his promises if he is elected prime minister in a May 1 general election, aides said on Wednesday
Blair himself has written the "contract", which forms the centrepiece of Labour's election manifesto which is due for launch at 9.30 a.m. (0930 GMT).

Labour, out of office since 1979, looks set to score a decisive victory over the Conservatives, although Prime Minister John Major was encouraged on Wednesday when an opinion poll put his party 14 points behind Labour against 18 a month earlier.
Aides said Blair, convinced that Britons are tired of politicians making and breaking election promises, restricts himself to pledges he is convinced he can honour.
"It's a What-You-See-Is-What-You-Get manifesto," one said. "John Major breaks promises, Tony Blair keeps promises. Tony Blair can be trusted to deliver."

Labour has mounted constant attacks on Major for promising to cut taxes at the 1992 election and then raising them. It says the broken Conservative pledges have resulted in an unhealthy cynicism about politics among British voters.

The party claimed on Wednesday that Major was at it again when he launched the Conservative manifesto with a surprise pledge to provide a fresh tax break to couples where one spouse quits work to look after children or elderly relatives.
In the contract, Blair repeats that Labour will not raise income tax rates and will provide stable non-inflationary economic growth.
He says education will be his government's number one priority, and the share of national income spent on it will rise.

And he repeats a promise to take 250,000 young people out of the dole queues, using proceeds of a windfall tax on surplus profits of water, gas, electricity and other firms privatised by the Conservatives.

Other pledges include more money for National Health Service patient care, the safeguarding of Britain's environment, a cleanup of politics following a bout of sleaze and to "the leadership in Europe which Britain and Europe need."

The 10-point programme, crafted to ensure that the Conservatives cannot attack Labour for profligate spending plans, contains no new promises compared with Blair's keynote speech to last October's annual party conference.
But aides said Blair would claim credit for this as showing he was consistent in his aims. "There has been no last minute panic attack. This is a proper programme for government," one said.
